story.headline: Swiss to vote on new nuclear plants
story.summary: Opponents filed over 125,000 signatures, forcing a national referendum on Parliament's move to lift the ban on building new reactors.
story.display_body: Opponents of new nuclear power plants have gathered more than 125,000 signatures — far above the 50,000 needed — forcing a national referendum on Parliament's decision to lift Switzerland's ban on building new reactors, the campaign said on Saturday 19 September. The "Nein zu neuen AKW / Non aux nouvelles centrales nucléaires" alliance — the Social Democrats, Greens, Green Liberals, parts of the Centre party and organisations including Greenpeace and the Swiss Energy Foundation — collected the signatures in three months and plans to file them with the Federal Chancellery on 6 October. In its summer session Parliament narrowly passed the Federal Council's indirect counter-proposal to the "Stop the blackout" popular initiative (whose backers have since conditionally withdrawn it), repealing the ban on new nuclear construction in force since 2018 under the Energy Strategy 2050. The committee accuses the government and Parliament of "governing against the will of the population," arguing voters have repeatedly chosen a renewables-based path. Once the Chancellery validates the signatures, the earliest the change could go to a vote is 28 February 2027.
story.why: For the first time since Fukushima, Swiss voters will decide directly whether the country reopens the door to nuclear power — a choice that shapes electricity supply, prices and climate policy for decades.

story.headline: Thousands march for climate in Romandie
story.summary: About 12,000 people marched in Lausanne and thousands in Geneva in a coordinated national climate mobilisation.
story.display_body: Around 12,000 people marched in Lausanne and thousands more in Geneva on Saturday 19 September in a coordinated national climate mobilisation. Police put the Lausanne crowd at roughly 12,000 — about double what organisers expected — while Geneva drew 7,000 by organisers' count and 3,000 by police estimate, with families, students and older residents in the ranks. An eight-chapter manifesto called for making "the climate emergency an absolute priority" and reshaping the economy to cut greenhouse-gas emissions. Further rallies are planned in Fribourg (20 September), Bienne (25 September) and Neuchâtel (2 October). The turnout lands as the nuclear referendum reopens a national fight over Switzerland's energy mix.

story.headline: Ukraine drones hit Moscow during Russia vote
story.summary: A large Ukrainian drone attack killed two and damaged a Moscow oil refinery on the final day of Russia's parliamentary elections.
story.display_body: A large Ukrainian drone barrage struck the Moscow region early on Sunday 20 September, killing at least two people and damaging a major oil refinery on the final day of Russia's three-day parliamentary elections. [ongoing since 2026-08-26]. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said air defences had intercepted more than 1,600 drones since Saturday, 450 of them bound for the capital, and that a facility at the Moscow refinery — hit repeatedly in recent months — was damaged again; he claimed the attack was timed to disrupt the vote. Regional governor Andrei Vorobyov reported two civilians killed and about 400 people evacuated from a high-rise set alight by a downed drone. In Ukraine, authorities said overnight Russian strikes killed at least four people in the Kyiv region, including three children. President Volodymyr Zelensky called the strikes' impact "very significant," saying they hit "one of Russia's key oil industry facilities." Al Jazeera's Moscow correspondent described it as among the largest single-day attacks on Russia since the war began. The barrage extends a months-long Ukrainian campaign against Russian energy and export infrastructure — after a strike on the Novorossiysk oil port on 9 September and disruption to Russian grain exports in late August — aimed at choking the revenue funding a war now in its fifth year.
story.why: Hitting Moscow's refineries during Russia's tightly managed elections is both an economic and a symbolic blow, testing how far Kyiv's deep-strike reach can strain the Kremlin's war economy.

story.headline: Oil slicks threaten Strait of Hormuz
story.summary: Greenpeace flags five oil slicks from tankers damaged by mines and missiles in and around the Strait of Hormuz.
story.display_body: Greenpeace has identified five oil slicks off Iran and Oman — at least one as large as Lake Geneva — leaking from tankers damaged by sea mines and missile strikes in and around the Strait of Hormuz, an environmental scientist warned on Sunday 20 September. [single-source]. Some of the vessels struck Iranian naval mines and others were hit by Iranian or US missiles during the ongoing Iran conflict, according to the report. The spills threaten protected coastlines of the Strait — the world's most important oil-shipping chokepoint — and of Oman, including mangroves and beaches that shelter green and hawksbill turtles, endangered Arabian humpback whales, dugongs, dolphins and migrating whale sharks. Cornelia Kienle of Switzerland's Centre Ecotox (the federal applied-ecotoxicology centre — ecotoxicology studies how pollutants harm ecosystems — attached to the Eawag water-research institute) told SRF the scale is hard to gauge because no reliable figure exists for how much oil has leaked, and that with the spills in an active war zone "there is no prospect of improvement" and volumes could rise sharply.
story.why: A war fought partly around the Gulf's key shipping artery is now spawning an environmental disaster there, one that could poison a rare marine ecosystem and further snarl tanker traffic.

story.headline: Bachelet quits UN chief race
story.summary: Michelle Bachelet withdrew from the race to lead the UN after a weak Security Council straw poll.
story.display_body: Former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet withdrew on Saturday 19 September from the race to become the next UN secretary-general, ending her bid to be the first woman to lead the organisation in its 80-year history. Bachelet, 74, announced the decision on Instagram after the Security Council's third informal "straw poll" (a non-binding test of support) on Friday 18 September gave her just one "encourage" vote against 11 "discourage," down from six encouragements in July. The same poll put Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan, who heads the UN trade-and-development body UNCTAD, in front with nine, ahead of Guyana's Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett on eight; the IAEA's (UN nuclear watchdog) Rafael Grossi, former Senegalese president Macky Sall and Ecuador's María Fernanda Espinosa remain in contention. A candidate needs at least nine of 15 Council members and no veto from the five permanent members before the General Assembly confirms them. Secretary-General António Guterres, whose term ends 31 December, has warned the body faces "imminent financial collapse," with $1.57 billion in unpaid dues at the end of 2025; world leaders gather in New York from Tuesday 22 September for the annual high-level session.
story.why: With an unofficial regional rotation favouring Latin America this cycle, Bachelet's exit reshuffles the contest to lead a cash-strapped UN deadlocked over Gaza and Ukraine — and narrows the field of women vying to break its all-male line of succession.

story.headline: US strike kills four in Caribbean
story.summary: US Southern Command says it killed four aboard an alleged drug-trafficking boat in the Caribbean.
story.display_body: The US military said it killed four people aboard a boat it accuses of drug trafficking in the Caribbean on Saturday 19 September, the latest in a campaign that has now killed at least 231 people. US Southern Command said "confirmed intelligence" showed the go-fast vessel was "actively involved" in narco-trafficking, but — as with most such statements — provided no evidence that it was carrying drugs. The strikes on alleged smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific have run since about September 2025, reaching at least 231 dead across 69 strikes, and UN experts and rights officials have repeatedly called them extrajudicial killings; the Trump administration is now pursuing deals with allied governments to extend the offensive onto land in Latin America.
story.why: Lethal force against unproven suspects at sea, without trial, marks a sharp and legally contested expansion of US counter-narcotics policy — one Washington is trying to widen further.
